item.title: Nusrat’s mother satisfied with HC verdict, seeks security for family
item.description:
Shirin Akter, mother of madrasah student Nusrat Jahan Rafi, on Monday expressed satisfaction over the High Court verdict in the widely discussed murder case of her daughter and sought security for her family, alleging that they have received threats.
“I am satisfied with the verdict, Alhamdulillah,” she told reporters at her home in the Char Chandia area of Sonagazi upazila in Feni following the verdict.
Shirin said some people had tried to portray Nusrat's death as a suicide after the incident. “But today's verdict has once again proved that it was a murder,” she said.
She alleged that they were threatened with arson attacks on their home and harm to family members, seeking security for her family from the authorities concerned, including Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
Sub-Inspector Palash Chandra Roy of Feni Model Police Station, who is part of the security detail, said additional security measures were taken around the family's home to prevent any untoward incident following the verdict.
The High Court on Monday upheld the death sentences of two convicts in the Nusrat murder case after hearing death references, appeals and jail appeals filed in the case.
The two convicts are Siraj-ud-Daula, expelled principal of Sonagazi Islamia Senior Fazil Madrasah, and Shahadat Hossain alias Shamim.
The court also commuted the death sentences of four convicts to life imprisonment and acquitted 10 others.
The lifers are Nur Uddin, Saifur Rahman Mohammad Jobayer, Jabed Hossain alias Sakhawat Hossain and Umme Sultana alias Popy.
Those got acquitted are Maqsood Alam alias Moksud, a former councillor and former general secretary of Sonagazi municipality Awami League; Hafez Abdul Quader; Absar Uddin; Kamrun Nahar Moni; Abdur Rahim Sharif; Iftekhar Uddin Rana; Imran Hossain alias Mamun; Ruhul Amin, president of Sonagazi Upazila Awami League and former vice-president of the madrasa; Mohiuddin Shakil; and Mohammad Shamim.
According to the prosecution, Siraj-ud-Daula sexually harassed Nusrat in his office on March 27, 2019. He was arrested after a case was filed over the incident.
On April 6, 2019, Nusrat was taken to the roof of the madrasah building after she refused to withdraw the case against the principal. Her hands and legs were tied, and kerosene was poured over her before she was set on fire.
Nusrat died on April 10 while undergoing treatment in a Dhaka hospital.
Her elder brother Mahmudul Hasan Noman filed a case with Sonagazi Police Station over the incident, which was later turned into a murder case.
On October 24, 2019, Feni Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal Judge Mamunur Rashid sentenced all 16 accused, including the suspended principal Siraj Ud Doula, to death.

item.title: PM for reviving girls’ stipends to curb dropout, child marriage
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday directed the authorities concerned to examine the feasibility of reintroducing universal stipends for girls from Class VI to the degree level, aiming to encourage them to continue their education and help prevent child marriage.
He gave the directive at a meeting on the Prime Minister’s Education Assistance Trust at the Prime Minister’s Office in the Cabinet Division of the Secretariat.
The meeting was informed in detail about the trust’s ongoing activities, its goals and role in preventing students from dropping out by providing financial assistance during their education, said Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Hossain Shadhin.
The impact and achievements of the universal stipend programme for girls, introduced during the tenure of former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia, were also discussed.
The programme was credited with helping increase girls’ school attendance, encouraging them to continue their studies and discouraging child marriage.
Against this backdrop, the Prime Minister asked the authorities to assess the possibility of reviving universal stipends for girls from Class VI to the graduation level.
He stressed the need for preparing a clear proposal after analysing the possible cost, number of beneficiaries, implementation process and expected social and educational impact of the programme.
The meeting also discussed providing stipends to boys on the basis of merit and eligibility to encourage them to pursue education.
Besides financial support, the meeting put equal emphasis on students’ nutrition and health as important factors for improving the quality of education.
Various aspects of the school-level mid-day meal programme, including its management, nutritional value and ways to ensure safe preparation and supply of food for children, were discussed.
The Prime Minister stressed that food provided to students must be nutritious, safe and of good quality, and said there should be no compromise over food standards.
The meeting also discussed two alternative approaches to implementing the mid-day meal programme, taking into account cost, management efficiency, local participation and quality control.
Tarique Rahman directed the authorities to launch pilot projects in two separate districts, with each district testing one of the proposed approaches, to assess their effectiveness, feasibility and potential outcomes.
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon, Prime Minister’s Education Affairs Adviser Mahdi Amin, Secondary and Higher Education Division Secretary Abdul Khaleque, PM’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon and other relevant officials attended the meeting.

item.title: Bangla QR transactions cross Tk110cr
item.description:
Following the mandate of Bangla QR under Bangladesh's 'One Nation, One QR' policy, the volume and total value of transactions have increased significantly.
While daily transactions averaged around Tk37 crore at the beginning of July, the figure surged past Tk110 crore last week.
According to Bangladesh Bank data, replacing proprietary QR codes of various institutions with the unified Bangla QR was made mandatory starting July 1 this year.
Since then, transaction growth on the platform has accelerated rapidly.
In early July, an average of 178,000 Bangla QR transactions occurred daily, accounting for purchases worth approximately Tk37.33 crore.
Last week, the average daily transaction volume rose to nearly 303,000, with the daily financial value reaching roughly Tk110.38 crore.
In effect, since the launch of the unified QR system, the daily number of Bangla QR transactions has nearly doubled, while the total transaction value has roughly tripled.
Meanwhile, on July 1—the day the unified QR policy took effect—the number of Bangla QR merchants nationwide stood at around 1.6 million.
That figure has now expanded to nearly 3 million.
Along with private commercial banks, state-owned banks are playing a lead role in expanding Bangla QR adoption.
Industry stakeholders believe that implementing a unified QR system across all banks and mobile financial services (MFS) will simplify digital payments and drive the country's transition toward a cashless economy.

item.title: ICT-2 sends 3 journalists to jail in crimes against humanity case
item.description:
The International Crimes Tribunal-2 on Monday ordered three senior journalists to be shown arrested and sent to jail in crimes against humanity case related to the July uprising in 2024.
The three journalists are former Bhorer Kagoj editor Shyamal Dutta, Ekattor TV managing director and editor-in-chief Mozammel Babu, and its chief correspondent Farzana Rupa.
Earlier, the tribunal had ordered the jail authorities to produce the three before it on Monday.
Prosecutor Faruk Ahmed represented the prosecution during the hearing, while prosecutors Zahirul Amin, Marjina Raihan, Tarek Abdullah and others were present.
Faruk Ahmed told the tribunal that production warrants were issued against the three journalists on August 17 in connection with the crimes against humanity case relating to the July uprising.
As they were produced before the tribunal on Monday, the prosecution sought to show them arrested in the case and send them to jail.
It also sought two months to submit the investigation report.
According to the prosecution, then prime minister Sheikh Hasina held a press conference at Ganabhaban on July 14, 2024 when some journalists made provocative remarks while asking questions.
Sheikh Hasina, in response, referred to the protesters as “children of razakars” and “granddaughters of razakars”.

item.title: Dengue: 3 more die, 994 hospitalised in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more people died of dengue and 994 new patients were hospitalised across the country in 24 hours until 8:00am on Monday.
With the latest fatalities, the dengue death toll has risen to 85 in the country this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
The new deaths were reported in Dhaka North and South city Corporations.
During the reporting period, 862 patients were discharged from hospitals after recovery.
Since January 1 this year, a total of 29,923 dengue patients were admitted to hospitals across the country. Of them, 27,758 have been discharged, while 2,080 patients are currently undergoing treatment.

item.title: Faridul: Regional engineering cooperation vital to tackle South Asia’s climate risks
item.description:
Greater regional cooperation based on science, technology and engineering expertise is essential to address the shared climate risks facing South Asia, Environment, Forest and Climate Change State Minister Shaikh Faridul Islam has said.
He made the remarks at a policy dialogue titled “Co-Design the Future of South Asian Climate Diplomacy,” organized by South Asia Regional Climate Cooperation (SARCC) at the CIRDAP auditorium in Dhaka on Monday.
The state minister said climate change does not respect national borders, making regional coordination crucial to addressing common environmental challenges.
He said the government has undertaken various initiatives to reduce climate vulnerability, including a program to plant 250 million trees and technology-based engineering measures to control pollution.
Highlighting the need to restore Dhaka’s rivers, he said an integrated master plan has been prepared to control pollution in the rivers surrounding the capital.
“Engineering-based drainage systems and stronger monitoring mechanisms are being implemented to stop pollution at its sources, particularly in the Buriganga, Shitalakkhya, Turag and Balu rivers,” he said.
Special Assistant to the Prime Minister’s Office on Environment, Forest and Climate Change Dr Md Saimum Parvez stressed the need to make SAARC and BIMSTEC more effective platforms for addressing transboundary climate and environmental challenges.
“Political commitment and technology transfer are crucial to preventing and managing transboundary natural disasters,” he said.
He called for stronger cooperation among South Asian countries in climate data sharing, disaster preparedness, early warning systems and adaptation technologies.
Professor Dr AKM Saiful Islam of the Institute of Water and Flood Management at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology presented the keynote technical paper.
He said climate change was no longer a future threat but a present development reality for South Asia.
“Heatwaves, flash floods, tropical cyclones, droughts, erratic rainfall, glacier melt and sea-level rise do not recognize geographical boundaries,” he said.
He stressed coordinated regional initiatives based on shared hydrological and meteorological data, saying timely information exchange on river flows, rainfall, floods, cyclones and other climate indicators could strengthen disaster preparedness and reduce losses.
Speakers said South Asian countries face increasingly interconnected risks to water, food security, agriculture, public health and livelihoods. They called for coordinated regional programs in river basin management, pollution control, climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction.
They also emphasized stronger cooperation among universities, research institutions, engineers, policymakers and civil society, with SAARC and BIMSTEC playing a greater role in joint research, technical cooperation and knowledge sharing.
Special guests included Jamail Bashir JB, member and technical expert of the National Tree Plantation Cell; Sharif Jamil, secretary general of Bangladesh Poribesh Andolon; Ziaul Haque, coordinator of the Least Developed Countries negotiating group; and climate negotiator M Hafizul Islam Khan.
Senior journalist Habib Rahman delivered the opening remarks. Other participants included representatives from the Human Safety Foundation, Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University, CCD B, IUCN Bangladesh, Helvetas Bangladesh, BRAC University, CAPS, YPSA and Unnayan Onneshan.
They stressed that stronger regional engineering cooperation, backed by political commitment and reliable climate data, would be critical to building a climate-resilient South Asia.

item.title: Is the US seeing a turning point in obesity rates?
item.description:
The United States has been grappling with an obesity epidemic since the late 1970s, but there is growing evidence that the constantly climbing obesity rates are beginning to drop.
“We’re seeing signs that there’s going to be a turning point,” said Benjamin Rader, an epidemiologist at Boston Children’s Hospital and at Harvard Medical School who conducts research into health trends using large datasets. In 2024, he and his colleagues published a study based on data from more than 16 million adults, which suggested there had been a decline in obesity prevalence in 2023 — for the first time in more than 10 years.
The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey also indicated a slight decline between 2021 and 2023. More recent surveys have also provided evidence of declining figures.
This comes as a series of new drugs, which some people are using for weight loss, have come onto the market. The use of the GLP-1 agonist drugs Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound has increased rapidly in recent years in the US, with prescriptions more than quadrupling between 2021 and early 2026.
Some of the active ingredients in these drugs were originally developed to treat Type 2 diabetes by mimicking a naturally occurring intestinal hormone to promote a feeling of fullness and to slow down gastric emptying. This has led to many patients losing a significant amount of weight.
For Rader, “it seemed like it [the impact of this medicine] was bound to show up in the data” and that it was possible to be “moderately confident that drugs themselves were having an effect.”
For Peminda Cabandugama, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for The Obesity Society, which provides support to professionals in the obesity field, “there is strong evidence showing that there is a significant decline in obesity.”
In a written statement to DW, he said the “general opinion is that GLP-1 medications and their combinations and their increased use as well as the recent attention put on the importance of weight management have played a large and direct role in this reduction in obesity prevalence.”
But for Rader there is no definitive proof of a causal relationship. He has no doubt that the drugs have led to weight loss in many people at an individual level, but he told DW that it was too soon to say whether it “will lead to a plateau, […] a decrease […] or a slower decrease in the next 20 years” and what the effect on the general population might be.
Cabandugama thinks the current figures might also have been influenced by lifestyle changes during and after the Covid-19 pandemic, and points out that “these trends are likely a confluence of multiple elements that include the increased use of anti-obesity medications, post-pandemic behavioral changes, increased awareness about the importance of weight management etc.”
Some researchers in the US don’t believe obesity rates will decline permanently. A study by the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington in Seattle predicts a rise in rates through 2035 and suggests that the proportion of obese adults could increase from 42.5% in 2022 to 46.9% in 2035.
Though Rader doesn’t necessarily consider such predictions to be wrong, he pointed out that many prediction models are based on data from before the boom in GLP-1 drugs and might not take into account their potential effects. In an article for the Journal of the American Medical Association, he warned that the models could overestimate the future burden of obesity.
The authors of the IHME study have not entirely dismissed this criticism, but they did point out that to date only a small proportion of obese people use such drugs and that many patients discontinue treatment within a year. They added that some people gain weight again after initially losing it, and more representative data was needed to assess whether such drugs will have a lasting effect on obesity rates.
Cabandugama has also urged caution, saying that while there are currently strong signs of a decline, “the general consensus is that it is still too early to tell whether this is a true trend reversal.”
Though for a long time, obesity was viewed primarily as a result of an individual’s lifestyle, it has since become well-known that this complex chronic condition is caused by a combination of biological, genetic, social and psychological factors.
If the US were at a turning point, the consequences would be far-reaching. Weight loss in obese people does not only reduce their risk of related health problems, but also contributes to greater mobility, more independence and a higher quality of life.
For Cabandugama, “the health outcomes to improve first would be betterments in cardiometabolic parameters: blood glucose levels (Type 2 diabetes mellitus), cardiovascular outcomes, fatty liver, obstructive sleep apnea etc.,” which in the long term could also reduce pressure on the healthcare system.
Regardless of whether rates are on the decline, Rader said “obesity still remains a huge public health crisis in America that deserves attention, deserves funding, and deserves alternative solutions, especially as we think about how GLP-1s are not accessible to all Americans based on price and other factors.”
“A turning point does not mean that we’re suddenly in the clear and that we don’t have to worry about this thing anymore,” he said.

Five types of advice you should never blindly seek from AI
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has become an everyday assistant for millions of people. From studying and writing to searching for information and solving everyday problems, AI can provide answers within seconds.
But that convenience can also make it tempting to turn to a chatbot for decisions that require professional expertise, personal context, or human judgment.
Experts warn that AI should not be treated as an unquestionable authority — particularly when the stakes are high.
A report by technology platform Mashable also highlighted concerns about sharing personal information with chatbots. A conversation may begin with a simple question before gradually moving into sensitive personal or medical matters, increasing privacy risks.
AI systems can also provide inaccurate information. In financial matters, for example, an incorrect answer could influence an important decision. Chatbots may also sometimes mirror or reinforce a user's assumptions instead of challenging them, potentially strengthening misconceptions.
Here are 5 areas where relying solely on AI advice can be risky.
When people experience unfamiliar symptoms, it can be tempting to ask AI to identify a possible illness or suggest treatment.
AI can provide general health information, but it cannot physically examine a patient, review every aspect of their medical history or perform diagnostic tests.
It should therefore not be relied upon to diagnose a condition, change medication doses, interpret serious symptoms or make emergency treatment decisions.
For medical concerns, consulting a qualified healthcare professional remains the safer option.
AI can be useful for understanding financial concepts, comparing options or explaining terms related to savings, loans and investments.
However, major financial decisions depend on factors such as income, financial obligations, risk tolerance and long-term goals.
Whether to take a large loan, invest substantial savings or make another major financial commitment should not be based solely on a chatbot's recommendation. Information provided by AI should be independently verified and, when appropriate, discussed with a qualified financial professional.
AI can explain legal terminology and provide general information about laws and procedures.
But legal decisions often depend on specific facts, documents, jurisdiction and recent changes in legislation. A chatbot may not have the complete context required to assess an individual case accurately.
Important matters involving lawsuits, legal notices, contracts or other significant legal decisions should therefore be reviewed by a qualified lawyer.
Talking to an AI about relationship problems can feel easier than discussing them with another person. A chatbot can help someone organise their thoughts or consider different perspectives.
But decisions involving marriage, separation, divorce, or major family conflicts require an understanding of emotions, history, and relationships that an AI cannot fully possess.
Instead of allowing a chatbot to make the decision, people should consider their own judgment and, when appropriate, seek advice from trusted people or qualified professionals.
AI can compare careers, explain job requirements, and help people think through the advantages and disadvantages of changing jobs.
But leaving a job or changing careers can have long-term consequences. Personal finances, family responsibilities, existing skills, job opportunities and future goals all need to be considered.
Before making such a decision, it can be more useful to assess your own circumstances and speak with experienced people in the relevant field.
None of this means AI needs to be avoided altogether. It can be a useful tool for gathering information, understanding options and preparing questions for professionals.
However, users should be careful about what they share with chatbots.
Protect personal information: Avoid entering sensitive details such as your full name, address, phone number, bank account information or national identification number unless absolutely necessary and appropriate.
Use general examples: When seeking information about a sensitive personal situation, consider asking about a hypothetical scenario rather than sharing identifying details.
Review privacy settings: Check the privacy and data-control settings of the AI service you use. Options for chat history, model training, and data retention vary between services, so users should review the specific platform's current settings and policies.
AI can make information more accessible, but speed does not always equal accuracy.
For important decisions involving health, money, law, relationships, or careers, AI is best used as a starting point for information — not as a substitute for professional expertise or human judgment.
The more serious the consequences of a decision, the more important it is to verify the information and seek appropriate human advice.

item.title: Manufacturers use high-cost alternative fuels to avoid collapse
item.description:
A severe, systemic natural gas outage across Bangladesh’s key manufacturing belts is pushing the nation's industrial foundation to its operational limits.
Deprived of normal pipeline gas pressure (10 to 15 PSI), factories across Narsingdi, Chittagong, Gazipur, and Narayanganj are either shutting down or burning expensive, non-traditional alternative fuels—ranging from raw wood and agricultural biomass to furnace oil and light diesel oil (LDO)—to keep basic machinery afloat.
With national pipeline pressure plummeting to near zero in major industrial zones, primary textile and heavy steel manufacturing capacity has crashed by 50% to 90%, inflating production overheads by up to 400% and threatening severe environmental damage.
Gas-dependent textile units report output drops of 70% to 90%; steel re-rolling mills have shut down nearly 40% of operations, while integrated steelmakers operate at just 30% to 50% capacity.
Switching steam boilers to furnace oil or LDO increases fuel overheads by up to 400% (4x) compared to grid gas, severely undercutting product margins.
Over 50 textile and sizing units in Narsingdi are burning timber in steam boilers at an extra cost of Tk10,000 to Tk12,000 per day, sparking environmental enforcement risks and deforestation concerns.
Mithila Textile Mills in Araihazar has successfully built a Tk50 crore ($4.2M+) rice husk gasification plant, generating 20,160 m³ equivalent fuel daily to cover 70% of its energy needs.
BSRM and other major steel producers warn that reduced billet output will collide with the October construction surge, driving retail rebar prices well above the current Tk81,000–87,500 per tonne.

item.title: Brac University students take social impact leadership to a new scale
item.description:
A growing movement of student-led social action at Brac University is set to reach communities across Bangladesh and beyond, with 156 students selected for the 2026 Millennium Fellowship to develop projects addressing some of society’s most pressing challenges.
For a fifth year, Brac University students will take part in the semester-long global leadership program, working on initiatives linked to education, climate action, health, gender equality, innovation, poverty reduction and other Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
Run by United Nations Academic Impact (UNAI) and the Millennium Campus Network (MCN), the Millennium Fellowship supports undergraduate students in translating ideas into time-bound community initiatives designed to create measurable social impact.
For Brac University, the fellowship reflects a broader commitment to connecting education with service, leadership and responsibility towards society.
The 2026 fellows will work on projects contributing to areas including SDG 4: Quality Education, SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities, SDG 13: Climate Action, SDG 16: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions, and SDG 17: Partnerships for the Goals.
Their work comes as Brac University marks its 25th anniversary, reinforcing a founding belief that education should not end in the classroom but should enable students to engage with real challenges facing communities.
Congratulating the fellows, Brac University vice-chancellor Prof Syed Ferhat Anwar said: “At Brac University, we believe education is most meaningful when it empowers young people to make a difference in the lives of others.”
“Seeing our students recognized for their commitment to social impact is deeply inspiring. Their projects reflect not only creativity and leadership, but also empathy, ethical responsibility and a desire to address challenges facing communities today,” he said.
The scale of Brac University’s participation has also grown significantly over the years.
The university’s first cohort comprised 14 fellows in 2021, followed by 22 in 2022, 26 in 2024 and 50 in 2025.
This year, 156 students have been selected — Brac University’s largest cohort to date and the highest number from any participating university worldwide.
The growth reflects increasing interest among Brac University students in using their academic knowledge, creativity and leadership to create change beyond campus.
Brac University registrar David Dowland, also co-chair of the Civic Learning Council of the MCN, said: “The Millennium Fellowship helps students connect what they learn with the needs of their communities.”
Globally, more than 76,000 young leaders from over 6,000 campuses across more than 170 countries applied to join the Class of 2026.
Around 330 campuses were selected to host more than 5,500 Millennium Fellows.
The Class of 2026 was launched through a Global Town Hall on 20 August 2026, connecting fellows from around the world.
Over the coming months, Brac University’s fellows will turn their ideas into action — working with communities, building partnerships and demonstrating how young people can use education not simply to prepare for their own futures, but to help shape a more equitable and sustainable one.

item.title: TUCSAA raises concern over possible syndicate in Malaysia-bound labor recruitment
item.description:
The Trade Union–Civil Society Action Alliance (TUCSAA) has voiced serious concerns regarding the recent finalisation of a list of 25 recruiting agencies for sending Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia, warning that it could pave the way for a new syndicate.

In a press release issued on Monday, the alliance acknowledged that reopening the Malaysian labor market presents significant employment prospects for Bangladeshis.

However, it cautioned that the selection basis for these 25 agencies, their exact mandate, and the mechanism for distributing job demands remain entirely opaque.

According to TUCSAA, following the Prime Minister’s visit to Malaysia in June, Bangladesh submitted a pool of 423 agencies meeting eight mandatory conditions.

The subsequent emergence of a 25-agency shortlist has triggered legitimate questions over how they were chosen and whether other qualified agencies will be sidelined.

Highlighting the bitter lessons of past recruitment cycles, the alliance stressed that high migration costs, irregularities, heavy reliance on intermediaries and the concentration of power among a handful of agencies previously exposed migrant workers to severe exploitation.

It noted that Malaysia itself canceled the licence of 49 recruiting agencies in July 2026 over syndication and irregularities, making transparency vital now to prevent any reconstituted monopoly.

While the government has stated that workers will be deployed via the state-owned Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) while engaging eligible private agencies, TUCSAA demanded immediate public clarification.

The alliance urged authorities to explicitly define the operational relationship between the 25 agencies and the BOESL-led framework before any recruitment begins.

To ensure accountability, TUCSAA outlined a series of demands, including the public disclosure of agency selection criteria, strict prevention of monopolies, clear caps on recruitment costs borne by workers, pre-departure verification of employment contracts and wages and the establishment of independent digital tracking and grievance mechanisms involving trade unions and civil society.

The statement was jointly issued by TUCSAA Member Secretary Jasiya Khatoon and Convener Shakil Akhtar Chowdhury.

item.title: Government has set examples of mismanagement and incompetence in 180 days: Nahid Islam
item.description:
The first 180 days of the BNP government have largely demonstrated ‘incompetence, mismanagement, shortsightedness and dishonesty’, said Nahid Islam, National Citizen Party (NCP) convener and the Chief Whip of the Opposition in Parliament.

He stated that the government is returning to old fascist and authoritarian structures. It has been proven in these 180 days that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has no plan whatsoever to run the country.

Nahid Islam made these remarks on Monday afternoon during an emergency press conference at the temporary central office of the NCP in Banglamotor, Dhaka. The press conference was organised by the Policy and Research Sub-Committee of the NCP to "highlight the failures of the ruling BNP government in its 180 days."

During the press conference, Nahid Islam read out a booklet titled "180 Days of the BNP Government: Return to Old Politics from Promises of Change—Mismanagement, Incompetence, Lack of Planning."

The booklet was written to mark the 180 days of the government. Assessing the government's 180 days overall, it was stated that immediately after assuming power, at the first cabinet meeting held on 17 February, the government set three priorities for 180 days. Keeping commodity prices under control, improving the law and order situation and normalising the supply of electricity and fuel.

After six months, data and ground-realities show that the government has failed miserably in each of these three priorities. Factories are closing down due to the energy crisis and workers are losing their jobs, while farmers are forced to buy fertilizers at high prices.

Evaluating the government, Nahid Islam said that the unprecedented crisis of fuel oil, gas and electricity has severely disrupted industrial production, the agricultural sector and the lives of ordinary people.

The prices of daily essentials have increased, loan sharks and looters of the banking sector are returning and old syndicates in the consumer goods and import markets have become active, with the BNP joining them as a new partner.

He also linked what he described as five months of inactivity by the Anti-Corruption Commission with the return of “looters and market syndicates”.

The Chief Whip of the Opposition noted that various reforms left behind by the interim government at the institutional level (such as the Human Rights Commission, the Enforced Disappearance Prevention Act and the Supreme Court Secretariat) are being canceled one by one.

He stated that in place of these, more ineffective and weaker laws are being formulated. Throwing the much-publicised 31 points and electoral manifesto into the bin, shameless politicisation and nepotism have been widely expanded in state institutions.

He stated that no visible progress is seen regarding the trials for the July genocide. Trials, medical treatment and rehabilitation of martyr families and injured individuals are absent from the priority policies set by the government.

Nahid Islam accused ruling party leaders and activists of continuously increasing attacks and filing cases against the opposition, differing opinions and journalists. He alleged that administrative officials are also facing harassment. He stated that in the vast majority of cases, instead of the attackers, the victims of the attacks are being legally harassed.

He alleged that the police are once again being turned into a partisan force. By not taking the oath of the Constitution Reform Council, the government has broken its electoral promise and the July Charter. The first 180 days of the BNP government have primarily created examples of incompetence, mismanagement, shortsightedness and dishonesty.

The booklet mentioned various topics across multiple chapters, including economic mismanagement, the energy crisis and the surge in commodity prices, disrupted production and job risks for workers due to the gas crisis, the electricity crisis and record load shedding, farmers' harassment and fertilizer shortages, economic misrule, bank seizures and market syndicates, increased costs and looting arrangements in mega projects, the cancellation of essential drug pricing policies, managerial failures during the measles epidemic, oppression of the opposition, interference in freedom of speech, harassment and cases against journalists, ignoring the public mandate of the referendum, politicization of state institutions, political nepotism and the RAB in a new guise. Detailed assessments of these issues were presented.

Government is 'failed', opposition is 'responsible'

During the press conference, top NCP leader Nahid Islam accused the government of returning to old fascist and authoritarian structures.

In response to a journalist's question, he said, "It has been proven in the first 180 days that Tarique Rahman has no plan whatsoever to run the country. He has merely assumed power and, according to old plans, according to the plans and policies of the fascists, he is running the country and driving it toward destruction."

Nahid Islam remarked that the government has utterly failed to establish the rule of law overall. On the other hand, he claimed that the 11-party alliance led by Jamaat-e-Islami, particularly the NCP as part of the opposition, has played a responsible role over the past six months.

Nahid Islam said, "We believe that we have behaved very responsibly from the position of the opposition. The change that should have been brought into the political culture has been brought by the opposition. The government has responded to that by gouging out the eye of one of our brothers. One person has died in Gaibandha and attacks are taking place in various places."

Nahid Islam views the propaganda that the opposition is actually failing or weak as a "tactic by the government to cover up its failures." He stated that they are constantly showing the people of the country where the government is making mistakes and breaking promises.

While they will demonstrate this to the people on a policy level, they will simultaneously resist it politically. If the government continues to walk that path, it will face a massive mass movement.

Nahid Islam stated that the 11-party alliance will soon hold long-marches across five to six divisions, followed by a grand rally in Dhaka. Through that grand rally, they will deliver a major message to the government.

Following that, if a stricter movement becomes necessary, they will announce it. Meanwhile, the NCP is also continuing its programs at the upazila, district, and metropolitan levels according to its capacity.

The India context

Regarding the press conference held in Delhi on 5 August by Sheikh Hasina, who was sentenced to death by a verdict of the International Crimes Tribunal, Nahid Islam believes it would not have been possible without the cooperation or backing of the Indian government.

He said that allowing the Awami League to conduct activities while simultaneously maintaining diplomatic relations with Bangladesh is actually impossible. They consider this to be conflicting and hypocritical.

Nahid Islam remarked that a new relationship must be established by re-evaluating India-Bangladesh relations over the past 15 years only upon receiving guarantees that Delhi will not allow the Awami League to conduct activities, will not harbor Sheikh Hasina there, that the Indian government will respect Bangladesh's judicial system and democracy and that the murderers of Osman Hadi will be handed back.

He stated that with the Ganges Treaty expiring this year, it is possible to establish a new relationship with India based on ensuring Bangladesh gets its fair share of water, preventing push-ins at the border, and stopping border killings.

Nahid Islam said, "Before these matters begin, if Tarique Rahman goes to Delhi once again where Sheikh Hasina is staying, what will that actually signify? How will the people of Bangladesh or the world view it? We believe this is not just about Tarique Rahman. It will be a humiliating event for Bangladesh. The message will go out that Bangladesh cannot stand tall in terms of an independent foreign policy or sovereignty."

NCP Political Council member Saleh Uddin Sifat conducted the event.

item.title: ‘Sustained pressure, security strategy vital for Rohingya repatriation’
item.description:
Bangladesh must maintain sustained pressure for the repatriation of Rohingyas, backed by coordinated diplomatic efforts and a credible, sustainable security strategy, Prime Minister’s Defence Adviser AKM Shamsul Islam said on Monday.
“The Rohingya crisis is not merely an issue for Bangladesh. It is also a humanitarian and security concern, a national security challenge at the diplomatic level, and a growing threat to regional stability,” he said.
He made the remarks as the chief guest at a seminar titled “Challenges of Rohingya Repatriation: International Politics and National Priorities”, jointly organised by the Department of International Relations and the Centre for Genocide Studies at the University of Dhaka.
The seminar was held at the Professor Muzaffar Ahmed Chowdhury Auditorium of the Faculty of Social Sciences. DU Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr ABM Obaidul Islam attended as the guest of honour, while Prof Dr ASM Ali Ashraf, chairman of the Department of International Relations, chaired the session.
Shamsul Islam said the government is committed to safeguarding Bangladesh’s security and sovereignty while doing everything possible to ensure the country’s development.
“Bangladesh has shown extraordinary generosity over the past nine years. But this generosity cannot be confused with an indefinite commitment to a single problem,” he said, stressing that Bangladesh did not create the Rohingya crisis and cannot resolve its underlying causes alone.
He said permanently shouldering responsibility for the Rohingyas is neither morally nor strategically acceptable for Bangladesh.
“Simply waiting and hoping that the situation will improve means that it will get worse every day,” he said.
The adviser said Bangladesh’s only viable option is to maintain active and sustained pressure for repatriation, supported by a coherent diplomatic approach and a credible security strategy.
He also called for stronger international cooperation to resolve the Rohingya crisis.

item.title: Hog Plum farmers log better business in Rangamati
item.description:
Hog plum is now in season across the hills of Rangamati, with trees laden with the popular sweet-and-sour fruit in homesteads, orchards and along roadsides.
For many Indigenous and Bengali communities, hog plum is more than a seasonal fruit. It has become an important source of income, particularly for women who collect the fruit and sell it in local markets.
The reddish soil and humid climate of Rangamati are considered suitable for hog plum cultivation. Local varieties are mainly grown in the district and require relatively little care. The trees can grow naturally around homes, along roads and on fallow land.
The fruiting season generally peaks during the Bengali months of Bhadra and Ashwin. Hog plum is green when unripe and turns light yellow as it matures.
The fruit is widely consumed across the district. Many people eat raw hog plum with salt and chilli, while ripe fruit is used to make pickles, chutney, juice and preserves.
Hog plum is currently being sold at Reserve Bazar and Banarupa Bazar in Rangamati town, as well as in markets across different upazilas. Retail prices currently range between Tk60 and Tk80 per kilogram.
Indigenous women vendors are bringing hog plum to town in baskets and selling it, helping supplement their household incomes.
Janki Rakhine, a hog plum vendor, said sales remain good during the season.
“Hoc plum sells well during the season. If government support and market access are increased, women in the hills will benefit even more,” she said.
Another vendor, Md Selim, said demand for the fruit is strong in local markets.
“Many customers buy both raw and ripe hog plum every day,” he said.
According to the Rangamati Agriculture Department, hog plum is cultivated on around 24 hectares of land in the district, with annual production estimated at approximately 240 tonnes. The potential market value of the production is around Tk60 lakh.
Rangamati Agriculture Officer Md Moniruzzaman said the agriculture department is assisting farmers by providing improved varieties of seedlings and necessary agricultural advice.
He also stressed the need for fruit-processing facilities to increase the value of locally produced fruits.
“Fruit-processing industries are necessary for value addition to all types of fruit. If processing factories are established in Rangamati, the district’s hog plum could eventually be exported beyond the country,” he said.
However, despite good production, a considerable amount of hog plum is wasted every year due to inadequate marketing and storage facilities.
Agricultural stakeholders say the establishment of cold-storage facilities and modern fruit-processing plants could reduce post-harvest losses and create new economic opportunities for hill communities.
With improved storage, market access and value-added processing, Rangamati’s hog plum has the potential to become an important contributor to the district’s rural economy while opening up opportunities for wider domestic and international markets.

item.title: Upstream water floods homes, croplands in Brahmanbaria
item.description:
A sudden surge of water from India’s Tripura state inundated low-lying areas of at least 15 villages in Akhaura upazila of Brahmanbaria on Monday, submerging croplands, fish farms and vegetable fields and forcing several families to leave their homes.
Residents said water began rushing into the area in the early hours of the day through the Haora River and the Jaji and Kalandi canals following heavy rainfall in the hilly areas of Tripura.
The flooding has affected low-lying areas of Dakshin Union, including Anwarpur, Hirapur, Abdullahpur, Dhaleshwar, Banger Char, Bautla, Birchandrapur, Sahebnagar and Umedpur. Several areas of Akhaura municipality, including Narayanpur, Taragaon and Dhatur Pahila, have also been inundated.
Low-lying areas of Mogra Union’s Colonel Bazar and parts of Moniand Union have also been affected.
Water has entered homes and business establishments around the Akhaura Land Port, disrupting the activities of small traders. Residents of some inundated homes have moved to relatives’ houses for shelter.
Farmers said they were particularly concerned about damage to their crops.
“After spending a lot of money and effort to cultivate paddy, I have now lost the entire crop to the floodwater,” said Abdur Rashid, a farmer from Abdullahpur. “If the water recedes, I do not know how I will cultivate the land again. The government should provide compensation to affected farmers.”
Monu Mia, another farmer from Birchandrapur, said his paddy fields were underwater and warned that continued rises in the water level could cause major losses.
Tajul Islam, a farmer from Rajendrapur, said around four kani of his paddy land had been submerged. He said the crop might still be saved if the water receded quickly, but prolonged flooding would cause significant damage.
Mahbub Mia, a small trader near the Akhaura Land Port, said water entered several shops and business establishments early yesterday.
“If the water continues to rise, the suffering of local residents will increase,” he said.
Abdur Rahim Mia, a member of Ward No. 8 of Dakshin Union, said heavy rainfall in the hilly areas of Tripura had caused the sudden surge of water, which entered Akhaura through the Haora River and the Jaji and Kalandi canals.
Several families have already been affected and taken shelter with relatives, he said.
Akhaura Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Tapasi Rabeya said the administration had assessed the initial damage caused by the influx of water from upstream.
“Thirty-two families have so far been affected, while around 1,400 hectares of cropland are underwater,” she said.
She said the administration was monitoring the situation and had kept local primary schools ready to be used as emergency shelters if the water level rose further.
Dry food, rice, relief materials and medicines have also been kept ready, she said.
However, officials said the situation had started to improve somewhat from the afternoon as the water level began to recede.
Local residents and officials said further heavy rainfall in Tripura could worsen the situation, while a continued decline in the water level could help limit the damage.

item.title: MAF urges Cyber Security Act changes to curb online abuse
item.description:
The Multiparty Advocacy Forum (MAF) has called for amendments to the Cyber Security Act, 2026, to introduce clear legal protection against technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV), saying the law does not adequately address online abuse.
The forum made the demand at a press conference at the Tofazzal Hossain Manik Mia Hall of the National Press Club, where it presented a six-point set of recommendations for a safe, inclusive and accountable digital environment.
Speakers said TFGBV should be recognized as a distinct and serious offence under the law. They said the Cyber Security Act, 2026, lacks clear definitions of TFGBV and “consent” and does not specifically address emerging forms of digital violence, including deepfakes, sextortion, cyberflashing, cyberstalking, doxxing and coordinated online harassment.
Speakers said TFGBV was not merely a cybercrime but a serious threat to human rights, personal safety and the equal participation of women and marginalized communities.
They urged policymakers to adopt the recommendations and make the Cyber Security Act more effective, victim-centered and responsive to emerging forms of digital abuse. They also called for active media cooperation to raise public awareness about TFGBV.
Members of Parliament Nadia Pathan Papon and Sultana Jasmine Jui spoke on the need to include TFGBV in the law and ensure legal protection for victims.
The written statement was presented by Sayra Chandra Chakma, joint general secretary of the central committee of Chhatra Dal, and Golam Mostafa, joint convener of the Bangladesh Youth Federation. The programme was moderated by Enzamul Haque of the NCP and Nasrin Rahman Popi of Chhatra Dal.
MAF Vice-President and Dhaka South BNP Joint Convener Saidur Rahman Mintu, MAF member and central Mohila Dal office secretary Shahinur Nargis, and leaders of various political parties also spoke.
The press conference was held under the B-SPACE project, implemented by Democracy International and funded by the United Kingdom’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO).

item.title: ‘Exceptional’ summer heatwaves in Europe hurting economies
item.description:
Across Europe, extreme weather is drying up rivers.
From the Rhine to the Danube to the Po, critical waterways are falling to record-low levels.
Cologne’s Rhine gauge sank earlier this month to its lowest reading since 1816.
At Kaub, one of the river’s shallowest stretches, the water level gauge fell ​to 6 centimeters two weeks ago.
The previous record low was 25cm in 2018. These rivers are small but critical arteries for inland navigation and transporting goods.
They also provide drinking water, cool power plants, generate hydro-electric energy and attract tourism.
Experts say this summer’s heatwaves are “exceptional” and the Rhine is at “breaking point,” and Europe’s economies will pay the price.
Rivers are reliable ways to transport liquid bulk, such as oil, gasoline and chemical products, as well as dry bulk, such as iron ore, coal and grain.
It is rare that operations across these waterways would be hampered, said logistics expert Rommert Dekker from Erasmus University in Rotterdam.
“But then if it happens, it has huge consequences because everybody’s used to it. There is no real backup,” he said.
When water levels on the Rhine River fell too low to carry the coal, chemicals and grains that Germany needed this summer, trucks took over instead.
All states in Germany, except one, were forced to temporarily ease a ban on trucks driving on Sundays.
Professor Dekker said Germany’s use of trucks and rail as an alternative to shipping was a costly way to transport products.
“Instead of one barge, you may need 200 trucks,” he said.
“Then production is reduced because of this, because things cannot be supplied.”
The cost to the EU economy is staggering, with Triodos Bank estimating this summer could cost $295 billion, equivalent to about 1 per cent of GDP.
The bank estimates that France will suffer the largest economic impact of extreme heat, and could lose 1.4 percentage points of growth, which would push the economy into a contraction.
The report found that the next most affected countries were Italy and Spain, followed by the Netherlands, which could suffer a 0.8% hit to its GDP growth.
Economist Ernst Hobma, who co-authored the bank report, said the freight sector was one of three key contributors to the economic damage.
“The smaller channels are already closed for shipping, simply because there’s too little water … they’ve become unnavigable,” he said.
“That’s caused disruption to supply chains for so many companies.
“All the companies sitting directly on the river and receiving inputs from them are affected.”
He said companies further downstream that relied on the supply chain flow were also being disrupted.
Water from the rivers is also critical for crop irrigation, and there are fears poor harvests amid the drought will push prices higher.
“We just know yields will be lower if you experience extreme heat and drought like we are in Europe today,” Mr Hobma said.
“That also will mean low yields going forward, probably pushing up food inflation and depressing GDP.”
European cereals association Coceral said the June heatwave alone had wiped out 9 million tonnes of grain crops, resulting in a 2 billion euro revenue loss for farmers, according to one estimate by the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit.
It is also harder to work when it is extremely hot.
“That’s most visible for people who work outside, so maybe people working in construction, for example,” Mr Hobma said.
“They simply need more breaks and maybe need to adapt their hours, if it’s even possible to do all the work that they had planned.”
The Triodos Bank report said reduced labour productivity was the largest contributor to the economic losses from heat, but was difficult to estimate.
“In poorly climate-controlled offices, we know that people perform cognitively less if it’s extremely hot,” Mr Hobma said.
“So all of these things together lead to labour productivity losses, and that adds quite some damage.”
Low water levels in the Danube in recent weeks have forced sharp restrictions at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant, with the river providing crucial cooling for its reactors.
In Romania, naval forces carried out a controlled explosion to blast apart a rock to divert water to the country’s last working nuclear reactor, but the plant was later shut down.
In France, where nuclear provides about 70% of the country’s electricity, reactors went offline due to a “massive influx of jellyfish,” a phenomenon made more common by rising sea temperatures.
“Power plants have had to shut down [or reduce output], and that raises electricity prices on those grids. And again, hurts economic activity,” Mr Hobma said.
Mr Hobma said shutting power plants while Europe was pushing for more domestic energy sources was a “double whammy” coupled with the wars raging to Europe’s east.
“I think that just shows that we need to build energy systems that are resilient even to more extreme climate scenarios,” he said.
“If we really want to become independent as Europe, we have to try to lower our energy demand as much as possible.
“So insulating homes, for example, contributes to that because we simply would need less energy to get the same quality of life.”
Professor Dekker said the cost of the impact to the nuclear power plants was running into millions of euros a day.
“We have to use gas and coal … that is really costly so that has a huge impact,” he said.
“There is a price to be paid.”
The global energy crisis fuelled by the war in Iran and effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has put pressure on oil supplies and the hip pocket of billions around the world.
Professor Dekker said the European heatwave would have a further impact.
“How much is due to the Iran crisis [and how much] to this long period of drought? It’s difficult to say … but definitely prices will go up.”
He said the cost to European tourism was also clear, with river cruises across the continent cancelled or disrupted.
This year’s drought across large parts of Europe has helped fuel devastating wildfires in France and Spain, with more hot and dry conditions forecast into September, according to the European Commission, with continued risk of heatwaves.
According to the European Drought Observatory, half of the EU and the UK is under drought at some level of intensity.
The World Health Organization said June data from five countries already showed nearly 10,000 excess deaths were linked to the extreme heat this summer.
University of Reading climate science professor Richard Allan said Europe’s recent extreme heat and drought signal that continued warming “will further intensify heatwaves, droughts and wildfires.”
It will also bring further flooding events from rising sea levels as ice melts and warmer oceans expand.
Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization.
“It is only by embracing long-term sustainable policies and practices that rapidly evolve our way of life to remove greenhouse gas emissions … that we can limit the mounting damage from our heating of the planet,” Professor Allan said.

item.title: This is how singles are actually falling in love in 2026
item.description:
If your dating life still runs on the old playbook — playing it cool, waiting three days to text back, never admitting you like someone — you are already behind. New research from Tinder and Plenty of Fish shows 2026 singles have rewritten the rules of romance, and the results are surprisingly wholesome.
The biggest shift, according to Tinder's data, is what researchers are calling "emotional vibe coding." More than half of singles surveyed said honest conversations matter most to them, while nearly half said they want more empathy shown after a rejection.
Translation: ghosting is out. People are done overanalyzing text messages and are simply saying what they mean.
First dates have changed too. Instead of an elaborate dinner, the trend is toward simple coffee walks and low-pressure hangouts — less performance, more actual conversation.
Another major trend is dating by committee. Tinder found that a large share of singles say their friends now directly shape who they match with, and many are going on more group or double dates as a result. The app's Double Date feature, which lets two friends team up to match with other pairs, has proven especially popular among women under 30, who are three times more likely to swipe right on a matched pair than a solo profile.
Plenty of Fish's trend report has coined the term "chemRIZZtry" — catching unexpected chemistry with someone a person did not initially expect to be into, due to charisma alone. About one in four singles say they have experienced this: falling for someone outside their usual type, purely because of personality.
The report also identifies "dating for the plot" — saying yes to dates less because of certainty and more out of curiosity. More than a third of singles said they had gone on a date purely for the experience.
Tinder's Chief Marketing Officer Melissa Hobley said: "Dating shouldn't feel like another deadline. Singles are looking for a connection that feels easy, honest, and a little fun."
After years of dating app fatigue, the shift toward honest conversation, low-pressure dates, and friend-backed matches suggests singles may finally be exhaling.

item.title: Draft NHRC law faces criticism over government control
item.description:
The draft National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) Act, 2026 has come under sharp criticism from civil society leaders, legal experts and human rights activists, who say government-dominated appointment procedures and prior approval requirements could undermine the commission’s independence.
The proposed law, while containing some positive revisions, also has internal contradictions and provisions that could restrict the commission’s ability to investigate rights violations independently, speakers said at a consultation in Dhaka on Monday.
The meeting, titled “Draft National Human Rights Commission Act, 2026: Review and Recommendations,” was organized by the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST) at Tofazzal Hossain Manik Miah Hall of the National Press Club.
Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman questioned whether the proposed selection process would produce a genuinely independent commission.
“Of the nine members of the selection committee, all except two remain under government control. Under such a structure, expecting an independent and neutral human rights commission is unrealistic,” he said.
He also criticized a provision requiring government approval to establish NHRC regional offices outside Dhaka, saying it could further undermine the commission’s institutional autonomy.
“We hope policymakers will reconsider these issues,” he said.
Nagorik Uddyog Chief Executive Zakir Hossain questioned why a body described as independent would require prior government approval to perform its functions.
“If an independent commission truly means independent, why should prior approval be necessary? Merely labelling it an independent commission does not make it one,” he said.
He also proposed that the commission’s budgetary allocations be made directly on the basis of its recommendations rather than through separate and potentially redundant funding mechanisms.
Human rights activist and former NHRC member Nur Khan Liton raised concerns over provisions requiring prior authorization for on-the-spot inspections.
“An investigation that requires prior permission holds no real value,” he said, pointing to what he described as contradictions in several provisions of the draft.
“We need a robust legal framework, but we also need to constitute a commission with honest and courageous individuals,” Liton added.
Supreme Court advocate Dr Kazi Zahed Iqbal highlighted potential legal complications involving evidence and compensation.
“There are critical questions regarding the evidentiary status of reports submitted by the commission in serious or criminal cases,” he said.
He also warned that the process of enforcing compensation could become caught up in bureaucratic delays and called for a separate, streamlined mechanism.
Sara Hossain, honorary executive director of BLAST and a senior Supreme Court advocate, called for a thorough parliamentary review of the proposed legislation.
“We want a well-thought-out Human Rights Commission Act. Section 19 has drawn significant debate given our lived experiences over the past two years,” she said.
She stressed that the commission must be capable of protecting the rights of all citizens, particularly marginalized communities, persons with disabilities and indigenous peoples.
Sara said BLAST would prepare specific recommendations and submit them to the Ministry of Law, while also making them available to the public.
Other participants called for reforms to make the commission more accessible and responsive to citizens.
Shireen Parveen Huq, founder member of Naripokkho and chair of the Women Affairs Reform Commission; Barrister Khan Khalid Adnan, a Supreme Court advocate; Satej Chakma, international affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Adivasi Youth Forum; author and researcher Anupam Debashis Roy; and Bhaskar Bhattacharjee, inclusion adviser at YPSA, took part in the discussion.
They called for digital complaint mechanisms and simpler administrative and management procedures so that people in rural areas, indigenous communities and persons with disabilities can access the commission’s services more easily.
Speakers said ensuring institutional independence, transparent appointment procedures and accessible complaint and investigation mechanisms would be crucial for the NHRC to function as an effective rights-protection body.

item.title: Study: Coastal salinity puts one in five at heart disease risk
item.description:
More than half of the drinking water sources in Khulna’s coastal upazila of Koyra have high salinity levels, while one in five adults aged 40 and above in Koyra and Satkhira’s Ashashuni face moderate to high risk of developing cardiovascular disease within the next decade, according to preliminary findings of a joint study.
The findings were presented on Sunday at a policy seminar titled “Drinking Water Salinity and Health in Bangladesh: Evidence, Adaptation and Policy Solutions” at icddr,b’s Sasakawa Auditorium in Mohakhali.
The study was conducted by icddr,b in collaboration with Imperial College London.
Researchers surveyed 27,697 water sources across 172 villages under 71 community clinics in Koyra and Ashashuni. Of these, 6,703 sources were used for drinking water.
The study found salinity in 55.3% of drinking water sources in Koyra, compared with 23.3% in Ashashuni.
Based on the findings, researchers proposed an integrated intervention package combining access to safe drinking water with primary healthcare.
The plan includes expanding access to low-salinity drinking water through community rainwater harvesting systems, pond sand filters and tube wells, alongside digital registries and routine monitoring of water sources.
The initiative also aims to strengthen the screening and treatment of hypertension, diabetes and chronic kidney disease through primary healthcare, supported by an algorithm-based clinical decision support system for screening, referral, treatment and follow-up.
Imperial College London Professor Adrian Butler said storm surges caused by tropical cyclones can lead to long-term salinization of ponds and shallow groundwater.
He stressed the need to restore water sources quickly after cyclones and maintain coastal polders and embankments.
icddr,b Executive Director Dr Tahmeed Ahmed said Bangladesh still has limited evidence on the links between climate change and health.
He said effective adaptation requires integrating safe drinking water, primary healthcare and community participation.
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Secretary In-Charge Fahmida Khanom said drinking water salinity is both a climate adaptation and public health challenge that requires coordinated efforts across the environment, health, water and local government sectors.
Dr Md Lutfor Rahman, director general of the Department of Environment, said research of this kind provides institutions responsible for environmental management with a stronger basis for policy action.
“We need to strengthen monitoring and generate data for evidence-based decisions on managing drinking water in salinity-affected areas,” he said.
Director General of the Directorate General of Health Services Professor Dr Pravath Chandra Biswas said there was already years of evidence on the links between salinity and health.
“The task is to bring that evidence together and translate it into practical guidance and policy, while strengthening prevention and management of non-communicable diseases through primary healthcare,” he said.
The seminar also highlighted the need for stronger water quality monitoring, health-based sodium guidelines for drinking water, greater inter-ministerial coordination and sustainable management of drinking water sources.

item.description:
By FE ONLINE REPORT

Bangladesh has expressed interest in joining the Mecca Joint Defence Pact signed this month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, the country’s foreign affairs state minister, Humaiun Kobir, said on Monday.

“We have expressed our interest in the Mecca Joint Defence Pact. Bangladesh recognises it, and there is an interest,” Kobir told reporters at the foreign ministry in Dhaka.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the defence agreement in Mecca on 7 August, establishing a framework for closer security and defence cooperation among the three countries.

Kobir said Bangladesh’s interest in such an arrangement should not be viewed as unusual, given the country’s close ties with Saudi Arabia and the wider Muslim world.

“Mecca has always held a special place,” he said. “Mecca is in the hearts of Bangladesh and its people. If a security alliance is formed among countries in the Middle East or the Islamic world, it would not be unusual for Bangladesh to join.”

His comments come as the government seeks to strengthen Bangladesh’s engagement with Muslim-majority countries while pursuing a broader foreign policy centred on strategic partnerships.

Kobir also said Bangladesh and India were working together to finalise the dates for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s proposed visit to New Delhi.

“The two countries are working on this. The dates will be finalised through discussions at a mutually convenient time for Dhaka and Delhi,” he said.

The visit would be closely watched amid efforts by the two neighbours to recalibrate their relationship and address outstanding bilateral issues through high-level political engagement.

Asked about questions surrounding his British citizenship and whether he had relinquished it before taking office, Kobir thrashed the idea, saying that he is a Bangladeshi citizen and those who are accusing him of having dual citizenship are against the interest of Bangladesh.

“I am Bangladeshi,” he said. “The very fact that I have come here and am working for Bangladesh means that.”

item.title: 40 beggars, vagrants held near Dhaka airport
item.description:
Police on Monday arrested 40 beggars and vagrants at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in the capital.

The Airport Police Station conducted the drive at the airport roundabout, BRTA station, Airport Railway Station, areas around police boxes, airport entrances and VIP Road, said Additional Deputy Commissioner (Media) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police Niaz Mehedi.

Police said the presence of beggars and vagrants in the airport area had long been causing inconvenience to local and foreign passengers, reports UNB.

Of those arrested, 15 were children, two were women, and 23 were adult men.

Police said steps were being taken to send the children to the Training and Rehabilitation Centre for the Vagrant in Mirpur, while the adults will be produced before a special court.

Airport police said around 288 more beggars and vagrants had been arrested in similar drives over the past several days.

With Monday’s arrests, the total number of people arrested so far stands at 328, police said.

Police said the detained children were sent to the Training and Rehabilitation Centre for the Vagrant in Mirpur, while the adults were sent to jail through the special court process.

The drives will continue to ensure the smooth movement of passengers and overall security in and around the airport area, police said.

item.title: Ex-home minister Mohabbat Jan dies
item.description:
By bdnews24.com

Former home minister Mohabbat Jan Chowdhury, who served under former military ruler HM Ershad, has died at the Combined Military Hospital (CMH) at the age of 92.

Mohammad Abdul Hoque, chairman of the Retired Armed Forces Officers Welfare Association (RAOWA) Club, confirmed his death on Monday.

He is scheduled to be buried at the military cemetery after funeral prayers following Maghrib in Uttara Sector 4.

Chowdhury joined the Pakistan Army as a second lieutenant in 1955 and retired as a major general. He also served as director general of the Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI).

After Ershad seized power, Chowdhury was appointed home minister in 1982, serving from July that year until July 1983.

Born in Gopalganj subdivision of Faridpur district, he later entered politics and won the Faridpur-3 seat in the 1986 election on a Jatiya Party ticket.

He also served as a director on the board of Micro Industries Development Assistance and Services.

item.title: Govt to launch post-accident emergency service on highways
item.description:
By FE ONLINE REPORT

FE Online

The government will soon roll out a post-accident emergency service on highways through 60 basic life-support ambulances, 40 motorcycle ambulances and 80 highway patrol motorcycles by providing post-crash medical services and highway patrol operations with the aim of halving road fatalities.

Under the project, 60 basic life-support ambulances will be deployed at 10-kilometre intervals along the Joydebpur–Hatikamrul–Bogura–Rangpur, Hatikamrul–Natore–Rajshahi and Joydebpur–Mymensingh national highways.

Under the multi-agency project -- Bangladesh Road Safety Project,-- the emergency vehicles will operate within 500-kilometer areas, supported by trained medical assistants and volunteers.

A ceremony in this connection was held at the Roads and Highways Department (RHD) conference room on Monday.

Road Transport and Bridges, Railways and Shipping Minister Sheikh Robiul Alam attended the event as the chief guest and said road accidents and resulting fatalities can be reduced by a half by 2030 if drivers and pedestrians are made more aware, effective enforcement of laws is ensured, and emergency medical services are provided promptly.

State Minister for Road Transport and Bridges and Railways Habibur Rashid, who attended as the special guest, said the programme marks a milestone in ensuring road safety.

He added that arrangements have been made to ensure that ambulances reach accident sites as quickly as possible so that speeding vehicles never bring human lives to a halt.

Project Director Sabbir Hasan Khan Ahmed said that operations for the post-accident emergency service will officially commence by September, with a joint venture operator providing the service for two years.

He noted that the vehicles will be available and monitored 24/7.

item.title: Nusrat murder: Mother satisfied with HC verdict
item.description:
By FE ONLINE DESK

Shirin Akter, the mother of madrasah student Nusrat Jahan Rafi, has expressed satisfaction with the High Court (HC) verdict in the widely discussed case over the murder of her daughter.

She also sought security for her family, alleging that they have received arson threats.

Shirin Akter was talking to the media at her house in the Char Chandia area of Sonagazi upazila of Feni on Monday, following the verdict, according to media reports.

She said, “Many people tried to term Nusrat murder suicide after the incident. However, with the verdict today, it has been proved once again that it was a murder. I am satisfied, Alhamdulillah.”

She further said, “We are being threatened that our homes will be set on fire. We seek security for our family from the Prime Minister and the authorities concerned.”

A High Court bench comprising Justice Bhishmadev Chakraborty and Justice KM Rasheduzzaman Raja on Monday upheld the death sentences for two convicts in the Nusrat murder case after hearing death references, appeals and jail appeals filed in the case.

The two convicts are Siraj Ud Daula, expelled principal of Sonagazi Islamia Fazil (Degree) Madrasah, and Shahadat Hossain Shamim. Besides, the court commuted death penalty for four other convicts to life imprisonment and acquitted 10 others.

The life imprisonment awardees are Umme Sultana Popi, Mohammad Nuruddin, shahadat Hossain Jabed and Iftekhar Hossain Rana.

Relatives of both the victim and convicts were present at the court during the verdict.

According to the prosecution, Siraj Ud Daula sexually harassed Nusrat in his office on March 27, 2019. He was arrested after a case was filed over the incident.

According to the case document, on April 6 in 2019, Nusrat was taken to the roof of the madrasah building after she refused to withdraw the case against the principal. Her hands and legs were tied, and kerosene was poured over her before she was set on fire.

Nusrat succumbed to injuries on April 10 while undergoing treatment in the burn unit of Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
