item.title: Connecting Bhola and mainland by road
item.description:
By FE

The decision to establish road communication between the geographically isolated island district Bhola and the mainland deserves all-round appreciation. Dependent on only waterway connectivity, mobility of both people and goods is very slow which becomes slower still during inclement weather. The communication gets snapped in time of natural calamities. So, the proposed road link is going to change all such limitations and restrictions. Considering the island's economic potential particularly after the gas find and extraction, construction of a highway connecting Bhola, Barishal and Dhaka is overdue. The envisaged road communication through Hijla and Mehendiganj will drastically slash the travel time between Bhola and Dhaka via Barishal. When the people's mobility accelerates, economy gets a mighty boost. There is no reason why this will not happen in case of Bhola that has so long remained isolated to a large extent. 

In countries like Norway and Japan, even remote islands including those valued for their tourism have been brought under road and highway networks. Bhola may not be a tourist spot but the prospect of its marine resources, in addition to its gas reserve, is quite bright. It stands to be a hub of exploitation of what is called blue economy. So this investment in the proposed highway unfolds limitless possibilities of contribution of Bhola to the country's economy. Even the current status of the island is quite lofty with the haul of different fish species including Hilsha. Sure enough, commercial fishing awaits development not only in the waters around the island but also in the coastal belt in the country's southern districts. Road communications will help develop the marine fisheries and supply chain to the mutual benefits of inhabitants of Bhola and other districts including the capital city. 

Although no details have been furnished about the schedule of feasibility study and undertaking the project, the prime minister's insistence on accomplishment of the task gives a positive vibe. Now that the decision has been made, the ground works should be started as early as possible. Issues like financing of the project and tender floating should be completed within a reasonable time frame. It would be expected that the plan is executed within the term of this government. In a country where even bridges over rivers and canals with the potential of serving people of 10-20 villages are left half or partially done, any project of highway connecting Bhola with the mainland must not be left destined to similar fate. The faster it is started and completed the better. 

Greater emphasis on road communication to the neglect of the railway in defiance of logic has made the country pay heavily in terms of archaic connectivity, environment and costs. The proposed extension of highway connection up to Bhola does not fall under that category of road communication. But it should include an option for railway connectivity in the future when Barishal is brought under the rail network. The merit of developing mass transport instead of pressing into service imported luxurious buses cannot be disputed. But Bhola's case is special and road connectivity will serve the purpose well. Connecting the island district with the mainland will be a milestone achievement.

item.title: Govt must break the cycle of recruitment syndicates
item.description:
By Mir Mostafizur Rahaman

For Bangladesh, the reopening of the Malaysian labour market should be a source of hope. It should also be a test of whether the country has learnt the lessons of the past.

News that only 25 recruiting agencies may be allowed to send Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia has caused concern among recruitment companies and migrant rights advocates. Their fears are not difficult to understand. Bangladesh has already seen what can happen when access to a major overseas labour market is concentrated in the hands of a small number of intermediaries: recruitment costs rise, competition is weakened and migrant workers can end up paying the price.

Malaysia is too important a destination -- and overseas employment is too important to Bangladesh -- for the country to risk repeating those mistakes.

Bangladesh has around 2,500 licensed recruiting agencies. Many have years of experience in sending workers abroad. Restricting access to Malaysia to just 25 agencies therefore raises a basic question: on what grounds are these agencies being selected, and why should the rest be excluded?

If there are legitimate reasons to limit participation temporarily, the government should explain them publicly. The criteria should be transparent, independently verifiable and applied equally. Otherwise, a measure intended to streamline recruitment could instead create a new system of privilege.

The concern is particularly serious because of Malaysia's history as a destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers. Previous recruitment arrangements were dogged by allegations of syndication, excessive fees, irregularities and the exploitation of workers. A small group of agencies and intermediaries was accused of exercising disproportionate control over recruitment, leaving prospective migrants with little choice but to pay high fees to secure jobs.

The consequences were severe. Workers -- many of them from low-income households -- borrowed money, sold land or mortgaged property to finance their journeys. Some reportedly paid far more than the officially prescribed migration costs. A job that was supposed to improve a family's economic prospects could instead leave it heavily indebted.

This is precisely why transparency matters now.

The Malaysian labour market is not simply another destination for Bangladeshi workers. It is one of the country's most important overseas employment markets. For decades, Malaysia has offered jobs to Bangladeshis in plantations, manufacturing, construction and services. A properly managed Malaysian market can provide thousands of workers with regular employment and a pathway to better incomes.

It also matters to the wider Bangladeshi economy.

Overseas workers are among the country's most important economic assets. Every year, millions of Bangladeshis working abroad send money home to their families. Remittances support household spending, education, healthcare and housing, while providing a crucial source of foreign currency for the country.

The importance of remittances becomes particularly clear when Bangladesh faces pressure on its external accounts. Money sent home by migrant workers helps strengthen the country's foreign-exchange position and supports economic stability. For millions of families, meanwhile, remittances are not an abstract macroeconomic statistic but the money that pays for food, school fees, medical treatment or the construction of a home.

Yet the contribution of migrant workers often begins with a considerable financial burden.

The cost of leaving the country can be extraordinarily high. Recruitment fees, travel expenses, medical tests, training and payments to intermediaries can consume a large portion of a worker's expected earnings. When recruitment is controlled by a small number of agencies, the possibility of excessive charges becomes greater, particularly where workers have few alternatives.

That is why the government should resist any arrangement that creates unnecessary concentration in the recruitment business.

There is a difference between regulation and restriction. The government has every right -- and indeed a responsibility -- to ensure that only competent and trustworthy agencies recruit workers for Malaysia. Agencies with records of malpractice should not be allowed to participate. But that objective does not necessarily require creating a closed group of 25 agencies.

A better approach would be a transparent accreditation system. Agencies could be assessed on their record, financial capacity, compliance with regulations, experience, worker-protection mechanisms and history of complaints. Those that meet clearly defined standards could be allowed to participate, while agencies that fail could be excluded.

Such a system would create competition without sacrificing oversight.

The recruitment process should also become far more transparent to the workers themselves. Before leaving Bangladesh, a migrant should know exactly how much the job will cost, who is paying which part of the recruitment expenses, what salary has been agreed, where the worker will live and what happens if the promised job does not materialise.

The government could publish approved recruitment costs and employer information online and require all payments to be made through traceable channels. Digital registration and complaint mechanisms could reduce the role of informal brokers, who often operate in the shadows of the formal recruitment system.

The agreement between Bangladesh and Malaysia should also be judged by what it delivers to workers, rather than simply by the number of people sent abroad.

A successful labour migration arrangement should guarantee that workers receive contracts they understand, wages that are paid on time, safe accommodation, access to healthcare and effective mechanisms for resolving disputes. It should also contain safeguards against contract substitution, forced labour and other forms of exploitation.

The government should make these protections central to its negotiations with Malaysia.

There is another reason for caution. Bangladesh is competing with other labour-sending countries for access to Malaysia and other international markets. If Bangladeshi workers become associated with high recruitment costs, opaque intermediaries and complicated procedures, Bangladesh risks losing its competitiveness.

A more transparent system, by contrast, could become a selling point. If Bangladeshi workers can be recruited at reasonable cost, through accountable agencies and under clear contracts, both workers and employers stand to benefit.

There should be no room for backroom deals or opaque decision-making.

The government must also establish strong monitoring mechanisms after recruitment begins. Transparency at the selection stage will mean little if agencies are subsequently allowed to charge workers excessive fees or use unregistered brokers. Regular audits, worker feedback, public disclosure of recruitment costs and swift penalties for violations should form part of the system.

Most importantly, migrant workers must not be treated simply as a source of remittances.

They are citizens whose labour sustains families and contributes to the national economy. They deserve a migration system that protects their dignity as well as their earnings.

Malaysia has the potential to become an important destination for a new generation of Bangladeshi workers. But reopening that market should not mean reopening the door to the practices that damaged it before.

Bangladesh has an opportunity to build something better: a recruitment system based on transparency, competition and accountability, where legitimate agencies compete on quality and compliance rather than access to political or administrative privilege.

The choice should be clear. Bangladesh needs more jobs abroad, but it does not need more middlemen. It needs higher remittances, but not at the cost of workers being pushed into debt. And it needs a Malaysian labour market that is open and sustainable, not one controlled by a handful of powerful interests.

The lessons of the past should not be forgotten. If the Malaysian labour market is to reopen, it must reopen in a way that puts Bangladeshi workers first.

item.title: Continental Hospital marks 20 years of patient care
item.description:
Continental Hospital in Gulshan marked its 20th anniversary on Monday with an event reaffirming its commitment to patient care.
Chairman Ahmed Ismail Hossain and Managing Director and CEO Malik Talha Ismail Bari inaugurated the event, along with board members, doctors, nurses, directors, and other senior officials.
Hossain said Continental Hospital PLC, one of Bangladesh's leading tertiary-care hospitals and a Joint Commission International (JCI)-accredited institution, is marking two decades of dedicated healthcare service, clinical excellence, innovation and commitment.
He said the hospital has become a trusted destination for advanced and specialized healthcare by combining modern medical facilities, technology, experienced doctors, skilled healthcare professionals and patient-centered service under one roof over the past 20 years.
Bari said: "Over the past 20 years, we have worked as the most reliable institution in the private health sector."
He said the hospital has treated more than 850,000 registered patients, 285,000 emergency patients and conducted more than 90,000 preventive health checkups.
Other milestones cited include more than 17,000 PET-CT scans, 36,000 successful surgeries, 45,000 gastroenterology procedures, 23,500 cardiac surgeries, 75,000 cardiac procedures, 450,000 cardiac consultations and 820,000 cardiac tests.
The hospital also provided radiation therapy to more than 230,000 cancer patients and dialysis services to more than 363,500 kidney patients, according to Bari.
He said: "Behind every number is a patient, a family and a story of trust. These milestones inspire us to remain even more committed to service — hence our slogan, 'We Care More.'"
As part of the anniversary event, a free preventive health checkup was held in the hospital lobby throughout the day for patients and visitors. The hospital also planted 20 trees of different species on its premises.
In the afternoon, the hospital organized Quran recitation, prayers and a milad for the well-being and long life of its patients.
